CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the theoretical foundations and core purpose of the Cognitive Walkthrough usability inspection method.
Identify appropriate task sequences and user goals for use in a Cognitive Walkthrough evaluation.
Apply the step-by-step Cognitive Walkthrough procedure to evaluate learnability in a user interface prototype.
Analyze interface designs to detect and document failure points that impede task completion.
Evaluate three peer prototypes independently using the Cognitive Walkthrough method.
Create structured documentation of Cognitive Walkthrough findings, including success criteria and usability issues.

Topics.Title: Foundations of the Cognitive Walkthrough Method
Topics.Summary: Introduces the theoretical basis and goals of Cognitive Walkthrough as a usability inspection technique focused on learnability and user cognition.

Elements.Title: What Is a Cognitive Walkthrough?
Elements.BodyText: A Cognitive Walkthrough is a structured usability inspection method in which evaluators simulate the step-by-step experience of a new user attempting to complete a task.
Elements.Notes: Unlike user testing, Cognitive Walkthroughs do not require participants — they are expert-based inspections that can be conducted early in the design process.

Items.Text: It is an inspection method, meaning it does not require real end users to participate.
The method focuses specifically on learnability — how easily a first-time user can accomplish tasks.
Evaluators walk through each interface action and assess whether a novice user would understand what to do next.
It was developed by Polson, Lewis, Rieman, and Wharton in the early 1990s as a cognitive science-based evaluation technique.

Elements.Title: Core Theoretical Basis: Exploratory Learning
Elements.BodyText: The Cognitive Walkthrough is grounded in theories of exploratory learning, which describe how users learn interfaces by attempting actions and interpreting feedback without reading manuals.
Elements.Notes: The method draws on research showing that most users prefer to explore interfaces rather than study documentation beforehand, making learnability a critical quality dimension.

Items.Text: Users tend to rely on recognition and contextual clues rather than memorized instructions.
Good interface design should support users in making correct guesses about what to do next.
Feedback and visible affordances are central to helping exploratory learners succeed.
The method evaluates whether the design supports this natural learning behavior at every step.

Elements.Title: Learnability as the Primary Focus
Elements.BodyText: Unlike broader usability evaluations, the Cognitive Walkthrough specifically targets learnability — the ease with which a new user can begin using an interface productively.
Elements.Notes: Learnability is one of Nielsen's five usability attributes. Focusing on it exclusively allows the Cognitive Walkthrough to produce highly targeted, actionable findings early in design.

Items.Text: Learnability measures how quickly a novice user can reach a basic level of performance.
The method is most valuable for interfaces expected to be used by first-time or infrequent users.
Recurring users who will eventually memorize workflows are a lower priority for this method.
Evaluators must maintain the perspective of a user who has never seen the interface before.

Elements.Title: Cognitive Walkthrough vs. Other Inspection Methods
Elements.BodyText: The Cognitive Walkthrough is one of several usability inspection methods, but it is distinguished by its narrow focus on step-by-step task cognition rather than broad heuristic compliance.
Elements.Notes: Heuristic Evaluation, by contrast, checks an interface against a set of general usability principles. Cognitive Walkthrough is more task-specific and cognitively detailed, making the two methods complementary.

Items.Text: Heuristic Evaluation is faster but less targeted at specific task flows.
Cognitive Walkthrough produces findings tied to concrete user actions and decision points.
Both methods can be applied to prototypes before any user testing occurs.
Combining both methods increases the breadth and depth of usability issues discovered.

Topics.Title: Preparing for a Cognitive Walkthrough
Topics.Summary: Covers the essential preparation steps required before beginning the walkthrough, including defining users, selecting tasks, and gathering materials.

Elements.Title: Defining the User Profile
Elements.BodyText: Before conducting the walkthrough, evaluators must establish a clear description of the intended user, including their prior knowledge, experience level, and goals.
Elements.Notes: A well-defined user profile anchors all subsequent evaluation decisions. Without it, evaluators risk applying their own expert knowledge rather than simulating a novice perspective.

Items.Text: The user profile should specify domain knowledge, technical familiarity, and motivation.
Evaluators must consistently adopt this persona throughout the entire walkthrough.
Assumptions about prior knowledge directly affect whether a failure is flagged or overlooked.
User profiles can be drawn from personas or user research conducted earlier in the design process.

Elements.Title: Identifying Task Sequences
Elements.BodyText: A task sequence is a specific, goal-oriented series of actions a user must perform to accomplish something meaningful in the interface.
Elements.Notes: Tasks should be realistic and representative of actual use cases. Avoid tasks that are too broad or too trivial. Each task should have a clear starting state and a defined successful end state.

Items.Text: Tasks must be written from the user's perspective, not in terms of interface controls.
Each task should have a clearly defined starting point within the interface.
Tasks should represent high-priority or high-frequency user goals.
Breaking complex tasks into numbered sub-steps is essential for granular evaluation.

Elements.Title: Gathering Required Materials
Elements.BodyText: Evaluators need access to the interface prototype, the defined task sequences, the user profile, and a documentation template before beginning the walkthrough.
Elements.Notes: If evaluating a paper or low-fidelity prototype, all screens and transitions should be available in sequence. Digital prototypes should be accessible in a stable, navigable state.

Items.Text: A documentation template ensures consistent recording across all tasks and evaluators.
All interface screens relevant to the selected tasks must be available before starting.
Evaluators should not modify the prototype during the walkthrough.
Having the user profile written down prevents drift toward expert assumptions mid-evaluation.

Elements.Title: Assembling the Evaluation Team
Elements.BodyText: Cognitive Walkthroughs can be conducted by a single evaluator or a small team, with each approach offering different tradeoffs in coverage and efficiency.
Elements.Notes: Research suggests that teams of two to four evaluators catch more issues than a single evaluator. However, the method is equally valid when performed independently, as required in this module.

Items.Text: Solo evaluations are practical and commonly used in academic and professional settings.
Team evaluations benefit from discussion at each step to surface differing interpretations.
All evaluators must apply the same user profile and task definitions for results to be comparable.
Evaluators should have basic familiarity with usability principles but not be designers of the product being evaluated.

Topics.Title: The Step-by-Step Cognitive Walkthrough Procedure
Topics.Summary: Walks through the core four-question framework applied at each action step, which forms the operational heart of the Cognitive Walkthrough method.

Elements.Title: Overview of the Four Evaluative Questions
Elements.BodyText: At each step of a task sequence, evaluators apply four diagnostic questions to determine whether a novice user could successfully complete that action.
Elements.Notes: The four questions were formalized by Wharton et al. (1994). They simulate the moment-by-moment decisions a user must make and reveal where cognitive breakdowns are likely to occur.

Items.Text: The questions are applied sequentially to every individual action step in the task.
A 'failure' answer to any question signals a potential usability problem at that step.
All four questions must be considered even if earlier questions suggest a failure.
The questions shift evaluator focus from interface aesthetics to user cognition and decision-making.

Elements.Title: Question 1 — Will Users Try to Achieve the Right Goal?
Elements.BodyText: The first question asks whether the user's current goal aligns with what the interface requires them to do at this step.
Elements.Notes: A mismatch here often indicates that the interface's conceptual model does not match users' mental models. For example, a user wanting to 'save' a file may not think to click an icon labeled 'Export.'

Items.Text: Evaluators must ask whether the design communicates the necessary sub-goal clearly.
Users may have the right ultimate goal but form an incorrect intermediate goal.
Vocabulary mismatches between user language and interface labels are a common source of failure here.
If this question fails, the interface likely needs clearer framing or labeling of the action.

Elements.Title: Question 2 — Will Users Notice the Correct Action Is Available?
Elements.BodyText: The second question evaluates whether the relevant control, link, or affordance is visible and perceivable to the user at the moment it is needed.
Elements.Notes: This question targets discoverability. Hidden menus, unlabeled icons, and low-contrast buttons frequently cause failures here. The action must be noticeable without requiring exhaustive search.

Items.Text: Controls that are visually prominent and contextually placed are more likely to be noticed.
Users scan interfaces rather than reading every element, so salience matters greatly.
Failure here often suggests a need for improved visual hierarchy or placement.
An action that exists but cannot be found is functionally equivalent to an action that does not exist.

Elements.Title: Question 3 — Will Users Recognize the Action as Correct?
Elements.BodyText: The third question asks whether users will understand that the available action is the right one to take to progress toward their goal.
Elements.Notes: Even if users notice a button, they must also interpret it correctly. Ambiguous labels like 'Process' or generic icons without text labels frequently cause failures at this question.

Items.Text: Labels and icons must clearly communicate what will happen when the action is taken.
Users rely on prior experience and conventions to interpret unfamiliar controls.
Failure here suggests the need for clearer labeling, tooltips, or contextual help.
This question distinguishes between noticing an element and understanding its function.

Elements.Title: Question 4 — Will Users Understand the Feedback They Receive?
Elements.BodyText: The fourth question evaluates whether the interface provides clear, interpretable feedback after the user completes an action, confirming progress or indicating an error.
Elements.Notes: Without meaningful feedback, users cannot tell whether their action succeeded or what to do next. This is especially critical in multi-step workflows where earlier errors propagate forward.

Items.Text: Feedback should confirm success, signal errors, or indicate that a process is underway.
Ambiguous or absent feedback leaves users uncertain and likely to repeat or abandon actions.
Error messages should explain what went wrong and suggest corrective action.
Positive feedback reinforces correct behavior and builds user confidence in the interface.

Topics.Title: Identifying and Documenting Failure Points
Topics.Summary: Explains how to recognize, categorize, and record usability failures discovered during the walkthrough for use in design improvement.

Elements.Title: What Constitutes a Failure Point?
Elements.BodyText: A failure point occurs when the answer to any of the four walkthrough questions suggests that a novice user would be unable or unlikely to proceed successfully at that step.
Elements.Notes: Not every friction point is a failure. Evaluators must judge whether a typical novice user — as defined in the user profile — would actually be blocked or misled, not merely slowed.

Items.Text: A failure is a step where the design does not adequately support the user's cognitive process.
Failures can range in severity from minor confusion to complete task abandonment.
The same interface element can produce failures on multiple questions simultaneously.
Evaluators should record failures even when they seem minor, as they may compound across steps.

Elements.Title: Categorizing Failures by Type
Elements.BodyText: Failures can be organized by which of the four evaluative questions they violate, which helps prioritize redesign efforts and identify systemic patterns.
Elements.Notes: Goal-alignment failures often indicate conceptual model issues. Visibility failures point to layout and visual design problems. Interpretation failures suggest labeling issues. Feedback failures indicate missing or unclear system responses.

Items.Text: Categorizing failures by question type reveals whether problems are structural or surface-level.
Multiple failures of the same type suggest a systemic design problem rather than isolated errors.
Severity ratings (e.g., low, medium, high) help prioritize which failures to address first.
Categorization makes findings more actionable for the design team.

Elements.Title: Writing Effective Failure Descriptions
Elements.BodyText: Each documented failure should include the task step where it occurs, the specific question it violates, a description of the problem, and the likely impact on the user.
Elements.Notes: Good failure descriptions are specific, evidence-based, and written from the user's perspective. Avoid vague statements like 'the button is confusing' — instead, describe exactly what the user would experience and why.

Items.Text: Include the task number, step number, and the interface element involved in every entry.
Describe what the user would likely think or do incorrectly, not just what the interface does wrong.
Link each failure to a specific evaluative question for traceability.
Suggest a potential redesign direction where possible, though this is optional.

Elements.Title: Using a Documentation Template
Elements.BodyText: A standardized documentation template ensures consistent recording of findings across all tasks, steps, and prototypes evaluated.
Elements.Notes: Templates typically include columns or fields for: task name, step number, action required, question evaluated, pass/fail status, failure description, and severity. Consistent formatting makes findings easier to compare and present.

Items.Text: Templates reduce the cognitive load of documentation during the evaluation itself.
Standardized formats allow findings from multiple evaluators to be merged and compared.
Every evaluated step should be recorded, not just those where failures occur.
Completed templates serve as a formal deliverable and audit trail of the evaluation process.

Elements.Title: Distinguishing Severity Levels
Elements.BodyText: Not all failure points carry equal weight; evaluators should assign a severity rating to help designers prioritize their remediation efforts.
Elements.Notes: A common three-point severity scale rates failures as: (1) minor — causes brief hesitation; (2) moderate — causes significant confusion or delay; (3) critical — causes task failure or abandonment. Severity should be judged relative to the defined user profile.

Items.Text: Critical failures prevent task completion and must be addressed before release.
Moderate failures create frustration and reduce user confidence even if the task is eventually completed.
Minor failures are worth noting but may be addressed in later design iterations.
Severity should reflect the impact on the defined novice user, not the evaluator's own experience.

Topics.Title: Applying the Method to Peer Prototypes
Topics.Summary: Guides students through the independent application of the Cognitive Walkthrough to three real peer-created prototypes, including practical considerations and ethical conduct.

Elements.Title: Understanding the Peer Prototype Evaluation Context
Elements.BodyText: Evaluating a peer's prototype requires maintaining an objective, constructive mindset, applying the method rigorously without personal bias toward the designer or design.
Elements.Notes: Students may feel reluctant to document failures in a peer's work. Remind them that the goal is to help the designer improve their product — identifying failures is a professional service, not a criticism of the designer's ability.

Items.Text: Findings should be framed as observations about the interface, not judgments about the designer.
Objectivity is maintained by consistently applying the user profile and four questions, not personal preference.
Evaluators should complete the walkthrough independently before discussing findings with the prototype's creator.
Peer evaluations provide valuable real-world practice that mirrors professional UX evaluation contexts.

Elements.Title: Selecting Tasks for Each Prototype
Elements.BodyText: For each peer prototype, evaluators must define or confirm at least one representative task sequence that reflects the prototype's intended primary use case.
Elements.Notes: If the prototype creator has already defined tasks, use those as a starting point but verify they meet the criteria for a valid Cognitive Walkthrough task — goal-oriented, clearly scoped, and decomposable into discrete steps.

Items.Text: Each task should reflect a realistic goal a user of that prototype would actually have.
Tasks should be decomposed into the smallest observable actions before the walkthrough begins.
If multiple tasks are evaluated, prioritize those with the highest frequency or consequence of failure.
Document your task definition as part of your submitted evaluation report.

Elements.Title: Conducting the Walkthrough on Each Prototype
Elements.BodyText: Apply the four-question framework to every action step of the selected task for each prototype, recording pass/fail outcomes and documenting all failure points.
Elements.Notes: Work through prototypes one at a time to avoid conflating findings. Take notes in real time rather than relying on memory after completing the walkthrough. Pay particular attention to transitions between screens or states.

Items.Text: Begin each walkthrough from the defined starting state of the task, not from the prototype's home screen unless specified.
Apply all four questions to every step, even when no failure is apparent.
Note any assumptions you make about what a novice user would think or know.
Record both failures and successes to provide a complete picture of the interface's strengths and weaknesses.

Elements.Title: Comparing Findings Across Three Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: After completing all three walkthroughs, evaluators should reflect on patterns across prototypes to identify common failure types and broader design insights.
Elements.Notes: Cross-prototype comparison is a valuable analytical skill. Students may find that certain failure types — such as ambiguous feedback or poor discoverability — recur across all three designs, pointing to common design education gaps.

Items.Text: Identify whether any failure categories appear consistently across multiple prototypes.
Note design decisions that successfully supported user cognition for use as positive examples.
Cross-prototype comparison strengthens your ability to recognize systemic usability patterns.
Reflections on cross-prototype findings should be included in your final evaluation summary.

Elements.Title: Preparing and Submitting the Evaluation Report
Elements.BodyText: The completed evaluation report consolidates all walkthrough documentation, failure descriptions, severity ratings, and reflective analysis into a structured deliverable.
Elements.Notes: Reports should be clearly organized by prototype and task. Include your user profile definition, task sequences, completed walkthrough templates, and a brief executive summary of key findings for each prototype.

Items.Text: Each prototype should have its own clearly labeled section within the report.
Executive summaries should highlight the most critical failures and their potential impact.
All claims about failures must be traceable to specific steps and evaluative questions.
Submit completed documentation templates as appendices to support your written findings.

Topics.Title: Interpreting Results and Communicating Findings
Topics.Summary: Covers how to synthesize walkthrough findings into actionable recommendations and communicate them clearly to designers and stakeholders.

Elements.Title: Synthesizing Findings into Patterns
Elements.BodyText: Individual failure points become more meaningful when grouped into patterns that reveal underlying design problems affecting multiple steps or tasks.
Elements.Notes: For example, if question 3 (recognition) fails repeatedly across a prototype, this suggests a systemic labeling or iconography problem rather than isolated errors. Pattern identification elevates findings from a list of bugs to a design diagnosis.

Items.Text: Group failures by the evaluative question they violate to surface recurring design weaknesses.
Patterns across multiple steps within one task suggest a structural interface problem.
Patterns across multiple tasks suggest a broader design philosophy issue.
Synthesized findings are more useful to designers than long lists of isolated issues.

Elements.Title: Writing Actionable Recommendations
Elements.BodyText: Each identified failure pattern should be accompanied by a concrete, feasible recommendation that the designer can act upon to improve the interface.
Elements.Notes: Recommendations should be specific enough to guide redesign without prescribing a single solution. For example: 'Replace the gear icon with a labeled Settings button to improve recognition' is more useful than 'make buttons clearer.'

Items.Text: Recommendations should be directly tied to specific failure types and their root causes.
Avoid recommending complete redesigns when targeted changes would resolve the failure.
Prioritize recommendations by the severity of the failures they address.
Where possible, reference established design conventions or guidelines that support your recommendation.

Elements.Title: Presenting Findings to Designers
Elements.BodyText: Communicating Cognitive Walkthrough findings effectively requires framing results constructively, focusing on the user experience rather than designer error.
Elements.Notes: In professional settings, evaluation findings are often presented in a debrief meeting with the design team. Framing matters: 'Users are unlikely to notice this button' is more constructive than 'you hid this button.'

Items.Text: Lead with the most critical findings to ensure they receive attention regardless of time constraints.
Use user-centered language that focuses on the novice user's experience, not the evaluator's opinion.
Provide evidence for each finding by referencing the specific task step and evaluative question.
Acknowledge successful design decisions alongside failures to provide balanced, credible feedback.

Elements.Title: Limitations of the Cognitive Walkthrough Method
Elements.BodyText: While powerful for identifying learnability issues, the Cognitive Walkthrough has recognized limitations that evaluators should acknowledge when interpreting and presenting findings.
Elements.Notes: The method's reliance on evaluator judgment means findings can vary across individuals. It also cannot surface usability issues that only emerge through real use over time, such as efficiency problems for expert users or issues related to data entry errors.

Items.Text: Findings reflect the evaluator's simulation of a novice user, not actual novice user behavior.
The method does not capture issues related to long-term learnability or expert-level efficiency.
Evaluator expertise and assumptions can introduce bias into failure judgments.
Cognitive Walkthrough findings should ideally be validated through subsequent user testing.
